question: How do Karpathy's autoresearch loop and AgentHub map onto Anthropic's workflow patterns, Dynamic Workflows and Knowledge Graph Construction Cookbook, and what staged path takes an engineer from one measured loop to a graph-grounded swarm?
hypothesis: Inferred from the text: the bottleneck in agent systems is often the placement of memory and evaluation, not the next model call.
contributions: Maps Karpathy's progression from autoresearch to AgentHub onto Anthropic's workflow infrastructure.
Treats the knowledge graph as the shared memory layer for multi-agent systems.
Provides a staged build path from one measured loop to a graph-grounded swarm.

limits: Anonymous, no publisher, no peer review; a secondary synthesis for study, explicitly not endorsed by Karpathy or Anthropic.
No original experiment: the staged build path (Day 1 to Month 2), exit criteria in Table II and the metrics in Table III are recommendations, not tested.

Cited sources are mostly GitHub repos, posts and press; several references lack authors, URLs or dates ([7], [11]). Reference [8] (Scaling Managed Agents) is listed but I did not find an in-text citation in the cached text; [11] likewise.

Authors concede: autoresearch does not equal frontier research; metrics can be gamed; AgentHub is 'a sketch'; dynamic workflows are expensive and produce correlated errors; fragmentation can reduce quality; entity resolution false merges are catastrophic.
Claims about Anthropic's 2026 features (Dynamic Workflows, 16/1,000 limits, ultracode trigger) rest on the cited post, which was not checked here.
practices: Start with one measured loop: take one LLM call with an evaluable output, add a stored first draft, evaluator with explicit criteria, revision step and stopping rule (Sec VI-A).
Add one tool only for a measured failure, with typed schema, permissions and result confirmation (Sec VI-B).
Use planning only when the task path varies; require a JSON plan, validate dependencies, cap retries and cost (Sec VI-C).
Go multi-agent with generator and critic first; every handoff is an artifact contract; reviewers return criterion-level defects; use worktree isolation for coding agents (Sec VI-D).
Begin the graph as versioned JSON or relational tables; extract with Haiku, resolve with Sonnet, attach provenance to every edge (Sec VI-E).
Scale to a swarm only for an embarrassingly parallel workload and define the reducer before fan-out; set concurrency, worker cap, token budget, timeout, retries, evidence contract (Sec VI-F).
Keep the commit DAG (work lineage) and the knowledge graph (domain knowledge) separate but linked (Sec V-A).
Build task-specific subgraph context within a token budget and with stable edge IDs for citation; do not dump the whole graph (Sec V-B).

Evaluate extraction (precision, recall, F1, schema-valid rate), resolution (pairwise P/R, false and missed merge rate, compression ratio) and queries (answer and cited path) against a gold set including adversarial cases (Sec VII).

Declare a complexity budget per run (model calls, sub-agents, tool calls, wall clock, tokens, cost, retries, graph writes); on exhaustion return the best artifact and the reason for stopping (Sec VIII-B).
Do not introduce a graph merely because there are agents; skip it when a relational table answers every query or no cross-session state is needed (Sec VIII-C).

Graph write invariants: every claim has a source or is marked inference; every artifact has an authoring run and version; every evaluation names a rubric; superseded objects stay addressable (Appendix).
